modules.title: Linux & Terminal Fundamentals
modules.description: Build command fluency and learn how shells translate intent into processes.

lessons.title: The shell is a program
lessons.summary: Separate terminal, shell, kernel, and command execution.
objectives: Read a command as program plus arguments
lessons.workedExample: Type `whoami`: the shell finds the executable, asks the OS to create work, and prints the result.
mistakes: Confusing a terminal emulator with the shell
Assuming every command is a shell builtin
lessons.recap: Connect the command or model to the OS boundary it exercises, then try a variation in the lab.

lessons.title: Compose commands deliberately
lessons.summary: Use quoting, exit status, variables, and short command chains.
lessons.workedExample: Run `mkdir lab && cd lab`: the second command runs only when the first exits successfully.
mistakes: Treating every space as a separator inside quotes
Ignoring exit status
lessons.recap: Connect the command or model to the OS boundary it exercises, then try a variation in the lab.

lessons.title: Expansion happens before execution
lessons.summary: Predict quoting, variables, globbing, and command substitution before a program receives its arguments.
lessons.workedExample: In `echo "$HOME/*.txt"`, quoting keeps the glob literal instead of expanding matching filenames.
mistakes: Assuming programs receive the original command line
Using unquoted variables for paths
lessons.recap: Write the expansion steps down, then test one change at a time in the terminal lab.

modules.title: Files & Directories
modules.description: Navigate a filesystem, compose pipelines, and reason about streams.

lessons.title: Paths are addresses
lessons.summary: Use absolute and relative paths without guessing.
objectives: Navigate safely with pwd and cd
lessons.workedExample: From `/home/student`, `cd ../shared` resolves to `/home/shared`.
mistakes: Using `rm` before checking pwd
Forgetting that `.` and `..` are directory entries
lessons.recap: Connect the command or model to the OS boundary it exercises, then try a variation in the lab.

lessons.title: Streams are process connections
lessons.summary: Use stdin, stdout, stderr, redirection, and pipelines as data paths.
lessons.workedExample: The left process writes bytes to a pipe while the right process reads them from stdin.
mistakes: Confusing > with |
Assuming stderr follows stdout automatically
lessons.recap: Connect the command or model to the OS boundary it exercises, then try a variation in the lab.

lessons.title: Links are names with consequences
lessons.summary: Compare hard links, symbolic links, and metadata changes through small filesystem experiments.
lessons.workedExample: Removing one hard link does not remove the inode while another directory entry still points to it.
mistakes: Expecting a symlink to survive its target
Confusing link count with file size
lessons.recap: Create two names for one file, change the target, and observe what each name resolves to.

modules.title: Users, Groups & Permissions
modules.description: Understand ownership and privilege boundaries through permission puzzles.

lessons.title: Read the permission triplet
lessons.summary: Decode rwx bits and calculate octal modes.
lessons.workedExample: 755 means owner rwx, group r-x, and others r-x.
mistakes: Treating directory write as file write
Using sudo instead of diagnosing ownership
lessons.recap: Connect the command or model to the OS boundary it exercises, then try a variation in the lab.

lessons.title: Privilege is a boundary
lessons.summary: Reason about ownership, sudo, umask, and least privilege.
lessons.workedExample: A directory can be readable but not searchable; access requires the execute bit on each parent.
mistakes: Using chmod 777 as a default fix
Forgetting group ownership
lessons.recap: Connect the command or model to the OS boundary it exercises, then try a variation in the lab.

lessons.title: Defaults are policy
lessons.summary: Use umask to explain why newly created files and directories start with different permissions.
lessons.workedExample: A requested 666 file with umask 027 becomes 640 because masked bits are removed at creation.
mistakes: Treating umask as a chmod command
Applying directory and file base modes identically
lessons.recap: Calculate the default first, then apply an explicit chmod only when the policy requires it.

modules.title: Processes & Job Control
modules.description: Watch programs become processes and learn how signals shape their lifecycle.

lessons.title: A process has a lifecycle
lessons.summary: Explore PID, PPID, states, signals, and wait.
lessons.workedExample: A shell forks a child, the child execs a program, and the parent waits for its status.
mistakes: Calling a program a process before it runs
Assuming kill always means terminate
lessons.recap: Connect the command or model to the OS boundary it exercises, then try a variation in the lab.

lessons.title: Signals are asynchronous requests
lessons.summary: Control foreground and background jobs without confusing signal delivery with termination.
lessons.workedExample: SIGTERM asks a process to exit cleanly; SIGKILL cannot be caught or handled.
mistakes: Calling every signal a kill
Losing track of the parent process
lessons.recap: Connect the command or model to the OS boundary it exercises, then try a variation in the lab.

lessons.title: When parents lose track
lessons.summary: Distinguish zombie processes from orphaned processes by following parent and wait relationships.
objectives: Explain why zombies retain an entry
lessons.workedExample: A child that exits before its parent calls wait remains a zombie until its exit status is collected.
mistakes: Calling every stopped process a zombie
Assuming an orphan is automatically stuck
lessons.recap: Trace PID, PPID, exit, and wait as separate state transitions.

modules.title: CPU Scheduling
modules.description: Operate a scheduler and compare fairness, throughput, and response time.

lessons.title: Why schedule at all?
lessons.summary: Translate workloads into scheduling objectives.
lessons.workedExample: A Gantt chart is a trace of CPU ownership, not merely a bar chart.
mistakes: Mixing arrival and completion time
Forgetting idle CPU intervals
lessons.recap: Connect the command or model to the OS boundary it exercises, then try a variation in the lab.

lessons.title: Preemption changes the trace
lessons.summary: Compare response, waiting, fairness, and context-switch tradeoffs.
lessons.workedExample: Round Robin trades longer completion for a better first response when the quantum is short.
mistakes: Comparing only turnaround
Forgetting context-switch cost
lessons.recap: Connect the command or model to the OS boundary it exercises, then try a variation in the lab.

lessons.title: Fairness has a clock
lessons.summary: Use response time and throughput together when judging an interactive scheduler.
lessons.workedExample: Response time is the first CPU start minus arrival, so a long job can still have a fast first response.
mistakes: Using completion time for response
Calling the shortest average wait universally fair
lessons.recap: Measure when work first starts and when it finishes; they answer different questions.

modules.title: Memory, Virtual Memory & Paging
modules.description: Trace address translation, page faults, and replacement decisions.

lessons.title: From virtual to physical
lessons.summary: Walk through pages, frames, and the TLB.
lessons.workedExample: A virtual address splits into page number and offset; the page table maps the page to a frame.
mistakes: Treating a page as a byte
Counting a TLB hit as a page fault
lessons.recap: Connect the command or model to the OS boundary it exercises, then try a variation in the lab.

lessons.title: Replacement is a prediction problem
lessons.summary: Compare FIFO, LRU, and Optimal on the same reference string.
objectives: Explain why Optimal is a bound
lessons.workedExample: Optimal evicts the page whose next use is farthest in the future—or never occurs.
mistakes: Counting a hit as a fault
Changing frame count mid-trace
lessons.recap: Connect the command or model to the OS boundary it exercises, then try a variation in the lab.

lessons.title: Too little memory changes everything
lessons.summary: Recognize working sets, page-fault pressure, and why adding multiprogramming can reduce throughput.
lessons.workedExample: If active processes need more frames than memory provides, the system can spend more time paging than executing.
mistakes: Treating every page fault as thrashing
Adding processes without checking locality
lessons.recap: Watch fault rate and useful CPU work together before changing a replacement policy.

modules.title: Synchronization
modules.description: Make race conditions visible and compare mutexes, semaphores, and monitors.

lessons.title: The critical section
lessons.summary: Find the exact region where interleavings become dangerous.
lessons.workedExample: Two increments can lose an update when read-modify-write operations interleave.
mistakes: Confusing concurrency with parallelism
Using a lock without naming its invariant
lessons.recap: Connect the command or model to the OS boundary it exercises, then try a variation in the lab.

lessons.title: Coordination preserves invariants
lessons.summary: Use a bounded buffer to see blocking, capacity, and condition signaling.
lessons.workedExample: A producer must wait when the buffer is full; a consumer must wait when it is empty.
mistakes: Treating sleep as synchronization
Checking capacity after mutation
lessons.recap: Connect the command or model to the OS boundary it exercises, then try a variation in the lab.

lessons.title: Wait for a condition
lessons.summary: Compare mutex ownership with condition waiting and make the protected invariant explicit.
lessons.workedExample: A consumer waits while the buffer is empty, releases the lock while waiting, then rechecks after wake-up.
mistakes: Using if instead of rechecking while
Signaling without changing the predicate
lessons.recap: Name the predicate, protect it with the lock, and recheck it after every wake-up.

modules.title: Deadlocks
modules.description: Detect unsafe states and practice Banker-style resource reasoning.

lessons.title: The four conditions
lessons.summary: Use a resource graph to reason about deadlock.
lessons.workedExample: Removing circular wait is enough to prevent deadlock even if other conditions remain.
mistakes: Calling every wait a deadlock
Checking only one process in a safe sequence
lessons.recap: Connect the command or model to the OS boundary it exercises, then try a variation in the lab.

lessons.title: Safe does not mean fast
lessons.summary: Run the safety algorithm and validate a resource request.
lessons.workedExample: A state is safe only if every process can finish in some valid sequence with current resources.
mistakes: Finding one partial sequence
Ignoring maximum claims
lessons.recap: Connect the command or model to the OS boundary it exercises, then try a variation in the lab.

lessons.title: Deadlock handling is a policy
lessons.summary: Compare prevention, avoidance, detection, and recovery instead of treating them as one algorithm.
lessons.workedExample: Detection allows flexible allocation but periodically searches for cycles and must choose victims when one is found.
mistakes: Calling an unsafe state a confirmed deadlock
Ignoring rollback cost
lessons.recap: Ask whether the system prevents, predicts, detects, or repairs the problem.

modules.title: Storage, Disks & Filesystems
modules.description: Connect file descriptors, inodes, mounts, and disk-head movement.

lessons.title: Names point to inodes
lessons.summary: Separate directory entries from file metadata.
lessons.workedExample: A hard link adds another directory name for the same inode.
mistakes: Assuming a filename is the file
Treating a symlink as a second copy
lessons.recap: Connect the command or model to the OS boundary it exercises, then try a variation in the lab.

lessons.title: Movement is a policy consequence
lessons.summary: Compare locality, fairness, and boundary behavior across disk schedulers.
lessons.workedExample: LOOK reverses at the last request rather than travelling to the physical edge.
mistakes: Mixing SCAN and LOOK
Dropping the return jump in C-SCAN
lessons.recap: Connect the command or model to the OS boundary it exercises, then try a variation in the lab.

lessons.title: Persistence has layers
lessons.summary: Connect mounts, caches, writeback, and fsync to what a successful write really means.
lessons.workedExample: A write can be visible to a process before fsync forces relevant data and metadata toward stable storage.
mistakes: Treating close as a universal durability guarantee
Assuming every path is on one filesystem
lessons.recap: Separate namespace visibility, kernel cache state, and durable storage.

modules.title: Shell Scripting
modules.description: Turn command fluency into repeatable, defensive automation.

lessons.title: Scripts are small programs
lessons.summary: Use variables, conditions, loops, and exit codes.
lessons.workedExample: A script should fail loudly when an expected file is missing.
mistakes: Unquoted expansion
Ignoring the exit status of a pipeline
lessons.recap: Connect the command or model to the OS boundary it exercises, then try a variation in the lab.

lessons.title: Automation needs failure semantics
lessons.summary: Use quoting, traps, exit codes, and defensive checks in Bash scripts.
lessons.workedExample: A script that deletes files should validate its working directory and input before acting.
mistakes: Unquoted glob expansion
Using eval on user input
lessons.recap: Connect the command or model to the OS boundary it exercises, then try a variation in the lab.

lessons.title: Scripts need experiments too
lessons.summary: Use test inputs, shellcheck-style reasoning, and controlled failures to make automation trustworthy.
lessons.workedExample: A script test should include a missing input, a filename with spaces, and a command that returns non-zero.
mistakes: Testing only the happy path
Depending on the current working directory
lessons.recap: Treat scripts as programs: specify inputs, expected status, and cleanup.

modules.title: Networking & IPC
modules.description: Explore sockets, pipes, signals, and safe communication boundaries.

lessons.title: Processes communicate
lessons.summary: Compare streams, datagrams, and shared state.
lessons.workedExample: A pipe is a unidirectional byte stream with a parent-child ownership story.
mistakes: Treating a port as a process
Forgetting framing in a byte stream
lessons.recap: Connect the command or model to the OS boundary it exercises, then try a variation in the lab.

lessons.title: Choose communication by ownership
lessons.summary: Compare pipes, FIFOs, signals, shared memory, and sockets.
lessons.workedExample: Shared memory is fast but requires a separate synchronization protocol.
mistakes: Treating shared memory as message passing
Forgetting framing
lessons.recap: Connect the command or model to the OS boundary it exercises, then try a variation in the lab.

lessons.title: Communication has failure modes
lessons.summary: Reason about closed pipes, interrupted reads, signal delivery, and partial communication.
lessons.workedExample: A writer may receive SIGPIPE when every reader closes the pipe, while a signal itself carries no byte stream.
mistakes: Assuming writes are always complete
Using signals for bulk data
lessons.recap: Choose a primitive based on whether you need data, notification, or shared state.

modules.title: OS Internals & Advanced Topics
modules.description: Tie user mode, system calls, interrupts, containers, and observability together.

lessons.title: Crossing into the kernel
lessons.summary: Understand traps, system calls, and privilege levels.
lessons.workedExample: A system call is a controlled entry point, not a direct jump into arbitrary kernel memory.
mistakes: Calling an interrupt a system call
Assuming containers are virtual machines
lessons.recap: Connect the command or model to the OS boundary it exercises, then try a variation in the lab.

lessons.title: The kernel boundary is observable
lessons.summary: Connect system calls, traps, interrupts, containers, and userspace observability.
lessons.workedExample: A system call transitions through a controlled entry path and returns with a status value.
mistakes: Assuming containers emulate hardware
Treating an interrupt as a syscall
lessons.recap: Connect the command or model to the OS boundary it exercises, then try a variation in the lab.

lessons.title: Observe before you optimize
lessons.summary: Use system-call traces, counters, and timelines to connect user behavior to kernel work.
lessons.workedExample: A trace can show repeated open/read calls even when the visible symptom is only a slow command.
mistakes: Measuring only wall-clock time
Changing policy before collecting a trace
lessons.recap: Build a small timeline first; then form one hypothesis and test it.

exercises.title: Find your bearings
exercises.prompt: Which command prints the directory you are currently inside?
exercises.explanation: pwd prints the shell process working directory.

exercises.title: Who interprets the line?
exercises.prompt: Which component parses a command line before asking the kernel to run a program?
exercises.explanation: The shell tokenizes input, expands syntax, and starts programs through OS interfaces.

exercises.title: Pipeline order
exercises.prompt: Which symbol sends standard output into another command?
exercises.explanation: A pipe connects one process stdout to the next process stdin.

exercises.title: Keep errors separate
exercises.prompt: Which redirection operator sends standard error to a file?
exercises.explanation: File descriptor 2 is standard error, so 2> writes it to a separate destination.

exercises.title: Decode 640
exercises.prompt: What octal permission gives the owner read/write, the group read, and everyone else no access?
exercises.explanation: 6 is rw-, 4 is r--, and 0 is ---.

exercises.title: Search a directory
exercises.prompt: Which permission lets a user traverse a directory and reach an entry inside it?
exercises.explanation: Directory execute permission allows traversal and name lookup when combined with the required parent permissions.

exercises.title: Lifecycle order
exercises.prompt: Which call replaces a process image with a new program?
exercises.explanation: exec replaces the current process image; it does not create a second process.

exercises.title: Ask before force
exercises.prompt: Which signal gives a process a chance to clean up before exiting?
exercises.explanation: SIGTERM is a request that can be handled; SIGKILL cannot be caught or cleaned up.

exercises.title: FCFS decision
exercises.prompt: For P1(arrival 0, burst 4), P2(arrival 1, burst 2), which process runs first under FCFS?
exercises.explanation: FCFS selects the earliest arrived ready process.

exercises.title: Quantum tradeoff
exercises.prompt: What usually happens when a Round Robin quantum becomes very small?
options: Response improves but context switches increase
exercises.answer: Response improves but context switches increase
exercises.explanation: A shorter quantum shares the CPU more frequently, improving first response at the cost of more switching overhead.

exercises.title: Page fault
exercises.prompt: What happens when a referenced page is not in a physical frame?
exercises.explanation: The OS handles the fault, often loading the page from backing storage.

exercises.title: Best possible replacement
exercises.prompt: Which replacement policy is an ideal lower bound because it knows future references?
exercises.explanation: Optimal evicts the page whose next use is farthest in the future and is used as a comparison bound.

exercises.title: Full buffer
exercises.prompt: What should a producer do when a bounded buffer is full?
exercises.explanation: The full-buffer condition blocks production until a consumer creates capacity.

exercises.title: Safe state
exercises.prompt: Which condition must be broken to prevent deadlock?
exercises.explanation: Preventing any one of the four necessary conditions prevents deadlock.

exercises.title: Calculate remaining need
exercises.prompt: In Banker’s algorithm, how is a process’s remaining Need calculated?
exercises.explanation: Need records the resources a process may still request before it can finish.

exercises.title: Head movement
exercises.prompt: Starting at track 50, how far does FCFS move to service 70 then 30?
exercises.explanation: The head moves 20 tracks to 70, then 40 to 30: total 60.

exercises.title: LOOK avoids empty travel
exercises.prompt: How does LOOK differ from SCAN at the end of a request run?
options: It reverses at the last request
It always jumps to track zero
It services only the nearest request
exercises.answer: It reverses at the last request
exercises.explanation: LOOK follows the current direction only as far as the last pending request, avoiding travel to the physical edge.

exercises.title: Exit means a result
exercises.prompt: What numeric exit status conventionally means a command succeeded?
exercises.explanation: Shell commands conventionally return zero for success and a non-zero status for failure.

exercises.title: Shared memory needs guards
exercises.prompt: What must accompany shared memory when multiple processes update the same data?
exercises.explanation: Shared memory provides speed, but mutexes, semaphores, or another protocol must protect concurrent access.

exercises.title: Controlled entry
exercises.prompt: What is the purpose of a system-call boundary?
options: Controlled transition from user mode to kernel mode
Direct access to every physical address
exercises.answer: Controlled transition from user mode to kernel mode
exercises.explanation: System calls provide a checked entry path into privileged OS services.

exercises.title: Quote the path
exercises.prompt: What is the safest way to pass a path stored in $FILE to a command?
exercises.explanation: Quoting prevents spaces and glob characters in the value from becoming extra arguments or expansions.

exercises.title: Hard-link identity
exercises.prompt: What do two hard links initially share?
options: A separate copy of the bytes
exercises.explanation: Hard links are directory entries that reference the same inode and underlying file data.

exercises.title: Apply umask
exercises.prompt: A file requested with mode 666 has umask 027. What effective mode is created?
exercises.explanation: The umask removes group write and all others permissions: 666 masked by 027 gives 640.

exercises.title: Collect the child
exercises.prompt: What removes a terminated child from the process table?
exercises.explanation: wait collects the child status and releases the remaining process-table entry.

exercises.title: First response
exercises.prompt: A process arrives at 4 and first runs at 9. What is its response time?
exercises.explanation: Response time is first start minus arrival: 9 − 4 = 5.

exercises.title: Spot thrashing
exercises.prompt: Which pattern most strongly suggests thrashing?
options: High page-fault activity with little useful CPU work
exercises.answer: High page-fault activity with little useful CPU work
exercises.explanation: Thrashing consumes resources servicing faults instead of executing useful instructions.

exercises.title: Recheck after wake
exercises.prompt: Why should a condition wait usually be inside a while loop?
options: Another thread may change the predicate before the lock is reacquired
exercises.answer: Another thread may change the predicate before the lock is reacquired
exercises.explanation: Wake-up does not prove the condition is still true, so the predicate must be checked again while holding the lock.

exercises.title: Name the strategy
exercises.prompt: Which approach allows requests only when the resulting state remains safe?
exercises.explanation: Avoidance evaluates a proposed allocation against a safety condition before committing it.

exercises.title: Visibility versus durability
exercises.prompt: Which operation is specifically used to request that buffered file data reach stable storage?
exercises.explanation: fsync asks the system to flush relevant file state toward stable storage; visibility alone does not guarantee durability.

exercises.title: Test the edge
exercises.prompt: Which input is especially important when testing a shell script that handles filenames?
exercises.explanation: Spaces expose unsafe unquoted expansion and argument-splitting bugs.

exercises.title: Pipe failure
exercises.prompt: What can happen when a process writes to a pipe after all readers have closed it?
options: It always creates a new reader
exercises.explanation: A closed read end can cause a write to fail and deliver SIGPIPE according to process handling.

exercises.title: Trace before tuning
exercises.prompt: What is the best first move when a command is unexpectedly slow?
options: Collect a focused trace or measurement
exercises.answer: Collect a focused trace or measurement
exercises.explanation: Observation narrows the cause before a policy change is made.
